# SK2044 — The equality members are inconsistent with each other

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A type declares one half of an equality or ordering contract and not the other: `operator ==` with no `Equals(object)` override, `Equals(Self)` with no `IEquatable<Self>`, or `==` and `IComparable` with no relational operators.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 1.3 |
| Supersedes | S1210, S3875, S3897 |

## Why

Each of the three is one decision written down once and not the second time, and each leaves two spellings of the same question giving different answers. `a == b` and `a.Equals(b)` disagree when only the operator was written, and which one a call site uses is a matter of style. A typed `Equals(Self)` that no interface advertises is invisible to `EqualityComparer<T>.Default`, to `Dictionary<Self, …>` and to every `where T : IEquatable<T>` constraint, so the type is compared through the object overload it was written to avoid — boxing on a struct, and identity on a class that has no override. A type that defines `==` and also orders itself, without `<` and `>`, offers half an operator set and sends the reader to `CompareTo` to find out whether the other half exists.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
sealed class Money {
    public decimal Amount { get; init; }

    public static bool operator ==(Money? left, Money? right) => left?.Amount == right?.Amount;

    public static bool operator !=(Money? left, Money? right) => !(left == right);
}
```

Write:

```csharp
sealed class Money {
    public decimal Amount { get; init; }

    public static bool operator ==(Money? left, Money? right) => Equals(left, right);

    public static bool operator !=(Money? left, Money? right) => !(left == right);

    public override bool Equals(object? other) => other is Money money && money.Amount == Amount;

    public override int GetHashCode() => Amount.GetHashCode();
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **One finding per type, in a fixed order, never one per sub-case.** The three are aspects of a single omission, and reporting them separately would multiply one decision by how many ways it shows. ⚠ **`SK2004`'s span is left to `SK2004`**: a type implementing `IEquatable<Self>` with no `Equals(object)` override is that rule's finding, and this one asks its precondition first and stays silent where it holds — by construction, not by a severity filter, so neither rule can be turned on into a duplicate. The typed `Equals` must take exactly the declaring type and return `bool`, so `Equals(string)` on something that is not a string is an overload rather than a contract; an explicit interface implementation counts as implementing the interface. Records are excluded, because the compiler writes all of it. The ordering half fires only on a type that already declares `==`, which is what separates a type in the operator business from the many that implement `IComparable<T>` so a `Sort` call works and want no operators at all. ⚠ **`S4035` — "classes implementing `IEquatable<T>` should be sealed" — is declined rather than implemented.** Unsealed is not the defect; the defect is an `Equals` that accepts a derived instance through an `is T` test, so that a base and a derived instance compare equal in one direction and not the other. That is a different analysis with a different false-positive story, it needs its own id and its own measurement, and a shape-only finding on every unsealed `IEquatable<T>` would report the many that handle it correctly. Fixless — adding `IEquatable<Self>` to a base list changes a public surface, writing `Equals(object)` needs to know what identity is, and an operator set cannot be generated from an ordering. Each is a review, not a text edit.
